channel.title: Research | Nikolai Alexander
channel.description: Quantitative studies of financial markets and options, with the data and the numbers behind each result.

item.title: Do most options expire worthless? Only the ones far from the price
item.description: How often calls and puts really expired worthless since 1990, depending on how far the strike was from the price and how long the option had to run. When the 90% claim is true, and when it is not.

item.title: The Santa Claus rally since 1950: up in 58 of 76 years, but the last three missed
item.description: In the 7 trading days of the Santa Claus rally, the S&P 500 rose in 58 of 76 years since 1950, by 1.25% on average. The pattern is real over the full history but has faded since 2000, and it missed in 2023, 2024 and 2025. After a miss, the rest of the year still rose in 13 of 17 cases.

item.title: Rolling the untested side of a strangle: which roll pays
item.description: Short strangles on SPY, QQQ, IWM, XLP, GLD and SLV, priced with each ETF's volatility index: in stock ETFs, rolling the put up after a rally added about 12% of the original credit up to 1 standard deviation but lost at 2. Rolling the call down after a drop only broke even if calls traded near the full VIX level, which they rarely do. Part 2 of 2.

item.title: Strangle defense: what happens after one strike is touched
item.description: Short strangles on SPY, QQQ, IWM, XLP, GLD and SLV, opened every day since 1993: after a touch the direction stays about as random as usual, but moves get larger, and a strike rolled at the usual distance is touched 1.4 to 2.4 times as often as it should be. How far to roll the other side. Part 1 of 2.

item.title: VIX term structure vs realized volatility: how much of the slope was premium
item.description: The VIX curve usually slopes up: since 2008, one-year S&P 500 options priced 3.9 points more volatility than 30-day ones on average, but realized volatility was only 1.4 points higher. What that meant for sellers at each term, and for puts vs calls.

item.title: Is the probability of touch really twice the probability of finishing in the money?
item.description: 469 S&P 500 stocks over ten years, the S&P 500 since 1990 and 18,462 earnings reports: a strike is touched about twice as often as it finishes in the money. Earnings gaps break the rule for calls and puts alike: a strike touched on the reaction day finished in the money about six times in ten. The trend splits the two sides: in the bear markets of 2000-02 and 2007-09, 59% of touched put strikes stayed in the money.

item.title: XLP for straddle and strangle sellers: five years of big moves that came back
item.description: Since November 2021 the consumer staples ETF XLP made 26 big turns where random versions of its own returns give 16 to 18, and after a 10% move from the entry day half of it came back in 84% of cases (random: 50%). What that meant for short straddles and strangles, and where the limits are.

item.title: The S&P 500 before the midterms: 19 of 19 cycles rose into the following year
item.description: Every US presidential cycle since 1949: the 2025-28 cycle is up 27.6% one week before the midterm, the third-highest of 19. From this point, the S&P 500 rose into the end of the following year in all 19 cycles. Strong starts gained less on average, but the link is weak.

item.title: 0DTE SPY odds: touched vs closed beyond, ten years of data
item.description: Ten years of SPY trading days, from the open to the close: how often a distance of 0.5%, 1% or 2% is touched, how often the close ends beyond it, and how the VIX, the weekday and the last day of the month change the odds.

item.title: Is delta the probability of expiring in the money?
item.description: Delta is often read as the chance of an option finishing in the money. The textbook model and four real option chains (SPY, Apple, Broadcom, Bloom Energy) show when that holds and when it does not.
